messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Transect Design for long term study
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Transect Design for long term study
messages.body_plain:
Andrea

There are several depths at which you could address this question.

- First, grab your handy copy of Buckland et al. (2001) and look at Section 7.8.3 that discusses trade off of permanent transects.  That sentence begins with the sentence "When the primary purpose of a survey is to monitor changes in abundance over time, greater precision is obtained by covering the same sample of transects at each visit (typically once a year)."  The section goes on to mention circumstances that might be exceptions to this.

- The section also makes reference to so-called "panel designs" where a portion of transects are retained over time but others are replaced by new transects.  These designs are described in N. Scott Urquhart and Thomas M. Kincaid (1999). Designs for Detecting Trend from Repeated Surveys of Ecological Resources Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics Vol. 4, No. 4, pp. 404-414

- There is mention of the subject in the context of 'repeated measures designs' in the recent book Buckland et al. (2015) in Section 3.2.4.  If your study involves not only grazed areas but "control" (ungrazed) areas, they you can consider Before/After/Control/Impact type designs, described with respect to fire in Buckland et al. (2009) and described in Section 7.4.1 of Buckland et al (2015).

- Section 8.5.2 of Buckland et al. (2015) discusses a more sophisticated analysis of the effect of conservation buffers upon bobwhites for fields with and without buffers.

This is a common problem people have when creating a coverage grid.  I most recently answered this question on 9 September 2014.  You could search the GoogleGroups email list for either the content of your error message "Error raised from: Distance.ClsGrid.SetDefault" or the cause of the error "LinkID" and you will find previous answers to this question.

You have not imported the shapefile of your study area properly. Read the Users Guide section in Chapter 5 entitled "Importing Existing GIS Data | Prepare the Shapefile"  that will tell you to create a field called LinkID in your shapefile to solve this problem.

messages.subject: Fitting a linear detection function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using distance sampling on aerial photos to quantify the abundance of whales. Photos were taken on each side of a plane at an angle of 27 degrees.  I am finding that the detection probability of whales decreases moving away from the track line. This results because the size of whales (in pixels) is smaller further away from the track line.  I think that the decrease in the detection probability is linear and that there is no shoulder close to the track line. Is there a way to fit a linear detection function in Distance (or in the associated R packages) and compare its fit to the standard detection function fitted by Distance? I was thinking that I could bin the data at intervals from the track line, and then run a linear model using the midpoint of each bin as the independent variable, and the number of whales within each bin as the dependent variable. From this model, I would obtain an AIC value and then compare it to the AIC values of the standard detection functions in Distance. Binning the data is not ideal because it is unclear what bin size I should use. I would prefer to use goodness-of-fit methods similar to the ones in Distance to compare models (linear vs the ones fitted in Distance) but I don’t know how to implement this in Distance (or in R). Does anyone have any suggestions on a method that would allow me to fit a linear detection function?

Thanks for your help,

Marianne

hello everybody,

with the help of distance team, the error was resolved. the shapefile which was copied to the .dat folder has value '0' (in arcmap) and 'null' in qgis in the LinkID field. (also keep in mind, LinkID field is case sensitive, so be careful while creating new field)  all you have to do is change the value to '1' and its done. if you are using arcgis, to edit field value you will have to start editor->start edit and then open attributes table and change the value. then click on save edits and stop editing.

also, after that, i had error with co-ordinate system. while designing survey you must keep in mind that the co-ordinate system of the project properties and the shapefile you have uploaded should be the same. for eg, it should be 'none' in both of them, or 'WGS1984' (in my case) in both.

i hope everybody finds it useful.

regards

messages.subject: Covariates in MR model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using an MRDS point independence model to analyze an io line transect survey. One of the available covariates is "species identification certainty", which is basically how sure the observers were of the species identity on a scale of 1 (certain) to 3 (very uncertain). Inclusion of this covariate as a factor does improve the MR model. However I am uncertain if it is appropriate to do so, because it seems somewhat tautological. If an observer is uncertain of species identification, it probably means that the sighting was a difficult one, which makes it less likely to be duplicated by the other team. In effect the observer is somewhat subjectively assessing the probability of duplication.

There is also the issue that the two observer teams often do not agree on the identification certainty, but the same problem exists for other covariates (e.g. cluster size) as well.

So my question is: is it appropriate to use a subjective judgement of sighting quality like this in an MR model, or should one stick to less subjective covariates such as weather condition, visibility etc.

Thanks in advance,

Daniel Pike.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Model Definition Properties for Mongolian Wild Camel Study
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Model Definition Properties for Mongolian Wild Camel Study
messages.body_plain:
Nice to renew your acquaintance again Moojii.  Looks as though you are putting your distance sampling training to use.

Your analysis highlights a subtle point when performing stratified analyses; I am not surprised you were confused by what you saw.  It makes such a nice example, I would like to be able to use it in some of our training materials if you would permit.

Here is my interpretation.  Post-stratification is assumed to take place over the same geographic area; you might remember the lecture notes from your 2011 training wherein we demonstrated post-stratification in association with two different species occupying the same study area.  We could use post-stratification to produce species-specific estimates and then we could add together the species-specific density estimates to produce a combined density estimate (this is how your second analysis was performed, look at the screenshot on page 5 of your document).

In contrast a 'regular' stratified analysis is thought to take place in geographically distinct portions of the study area.  Stratum-specific density estimates are produced by Distance, but then the question becomes how to combine those stratum-specific estimates?  There are several ways to define the combination in Distance.

It makes most sense to take the average of the stratum-specific densities as an estimate of the density in the entire study area (the densities of the two regions should not be added together).  But there are different ways to calculate an average.  Looking at page 3 of the document you attached, you asked Distance to produce an estimate for the entire study area as the mean of the stratum-specific estimates weighted by the area of the strata.  I believe this is not the proper weighting to apply because the size of the "Limited" stratum is quite large (>20000km^2) but you have very little sampling effort in that stratum.  I would consider using weighting by "effort" which you can select in Distance, as being a more appropriate weighting scheme.  Weighting by effort places more weight on the strata where there was more sampling effort and less weight in less-intensively studied regions.

In the final assessment, the conclusive analysis is based upon your judgement, specifically regarding the information you gathered from the outer (limited) zone.  I would be reluctant to make inference to 20000km^2 based upon 9 sampling points all of which are clustered in the northern portion of this region.  I would be inclined to remove the limited zone from your analysis (as you did in analysis 3) because of the limited information you have for that stratum.

You then need to decide whether the resulting overall density estimate should be the weighted average of the 2 (core and conservation) strata and whether the weighting should be by stratum size (the result you have for analysis 3) or weighted by sampling effort.  Given you have 32 points in each core and conservation, it is easy to calculate by hand that this alternative weighting produces an overall density estimate of 0.0192 per km^2 (compared to the 0.0204 per km^2 in analysis 3).  This mean density translates to an estimated camel abundance of 496 using the weighting by effort compared to 527 weighting by area.  The difference between those two values is small (6%) relative to the size of the respective coefficients of variation (~40%).

I hope that helps you with your analysis.  Good for you to have completed the survey and diagnosed a curiosity with your analysis.

messages.subject: Adding output to Analysis Browser
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

I have run an analysis using the MCDS analysis engine in Distance. I'd like to have results from a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and estimate of deviance explained. I added these to the analysis browser window, but the program doesn't seem to want to give me the output. No results are present in the analysis tab of the project browser, and I searched in the exported stats file and it gives me nothing other than the output that comes as default when one downloads the Distance package (1-6: #params, delta aic, aic, D, DLCL, DUCL). I've tried closing Distance and starting a new project to re-run the analysis, re-installing the software, upgrading to 7.0, running on another computer, and searching through the posts on the forum, in the Distance 6.0 user guide, and Buckland et al. 2015. I'm so sorry if there is something obvious I'm missing here. Thanks in advance for any direction you may be able to give me about how I can fix this issue!

Lani

You've not described the type of data you are trying to analyse, but from your description of your difficulty, I suspect that the data you are analysing is not capable of providing the output statistics you describe.

The KS test can only be computed with exact distance (not binned) data.  Likewise, deviance explained is only relevant when performing density surface modelling.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] funtion nb not found
messages.body_plain:
Sarah

I see you are trying to duplicate the sperm whale analysis described by Dave Miller in his spatial modelling workshop exercises.  I don't see any syntax errors in the code you have provide, I am left to suggest that perhaps you might not have the most recent version of the mgcv package to apply the negative binomial.  I'm not sure when nb() came into mgcv, but simplest to update all the necessary packages via:

install.packages(c("Distance", "dsm", "ggplot2", "knitr", "plyr",
                   "raster", "reshape2", "rgdal", "viridis",
                   "htmltools", "caTools", "bitops", "rmarkdown",
                   "tweedie"))

Hope that is useful.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am currently struggling with this problem. My ESW is a few meters. My grid cells are 30m. I have produced a DSM but my model is terrible. I really think that my segments are too small (4 meters or so) which means I have a ton of segments (each transect is 2km and I have close to 200 transects.  This results in several segment centroids being on the same pixel and thus having the same value leading to data clumping. My next step is to split the transects into 90m segments which would give at least a pixel between each centroid. Is this a bad idea? Any suggestions?

Sarah

On Sunday, August 10, 2014 at 10:00:51 AM UTC-4, Eric Rexstad wrote:
> Good questions Adrian.
>

As you note, often the covariate data you wish to use are from other studies, unrelated to your organism.  This can result in a heterogeneous assemblage of data, none of which was necessarily collected for the use you will put it to.  You would like to use a spatial resolution that is relevant to your study organism.

>
>

> > There is a recommendation that the segment should have twice the ESW or the strip band width in length.
> >
> > On the other hand, environmental covariables may come from different sources with different resolutions: for exampe, a Digital Elevation Model comes with a 90m resolution and NDVI data from MODIS comes in 250m resolution. Even when we can average this values under a segment of a larger size, one would expect that using a smaller grid cell size would produce a more precise abundance estimate, but surely there is a trade-off.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sarah,

What do you mean with "terrible model"? Poor deviance explained? Crazy extrapolation in numbers?

Besides the issue you mention, that may lead to some kind of pseudo replication of segments and their subsequent covariates, I wonder if your transects sampled the range of the covariates used for the model.

Sometimes if you sample part of the range and you find a good relation, when you extrapolate to the whole range you may obtain wierd extrapolations, together with large CVs.

It will also help to understand that you let us know the objet of the study and the area where you want to estimate.

I really think that my segments are too small (4 meters or so) which means I have a ton of segments (each transect is 2km and I have close to 200 transects.  This results in several segment centroids being on the same pixel and thus having the same value leading to data clumping. My next step is to split the transects into 90m segments which would give at least a pixel between each centroid. Is this a bad idea? Any suggestions?
>
> Sarah
>
> On Sunday, August 10, 2014 at 10:00:51 AM UTC-4, Eric Rexstad wrote:
> > Good questions Adrian.
> >
> > We do not have 'conventional wisdom' on this subject that differs from yours.  You have touched on the important topics.  As you note, often the covariate data you wish to use are from other studies, unrelated to your organism.  This can result in a heterogeneous assemblage of data, none of which was necessarily collected for the use you will put it to.  You would like to use a spatial resolution that is relevant to your study organism.
> >
> > Anxious to hear what arises from this discussion.
> >
> >
> > On 08/08/2014 20:40, Adrian Schiavini wrote:
> > > Hi everybody,
> > >
> > > I wonder if there is a rule of thumb regarding the relationship between the size of the segment (when you split the transect in segments) and the cell size for the prediction grid.
> > >
> > > There is a recommendation that the segment should have twice the ESW or the strip band width in length.
> > >
> > > On the other hand, environmental covariables may come from different sources with different resolutions: for exampe, a Digital Elevation Model comes with a 90m resolution and NDVI data from MODIS comes in 250m resolution. Even when we can average this values under a segment of a larger size, one would expect that using a smaller grid cell size would produce a more precise abundance estimate, but surely there is a trade-off.
